O Prophet! A address that honours him, for He addressed him with prophethood, whereas He addressed the rest of the prophets by their names. ﴿O Prophet, fear God﴾, that is, persist in piety and increase in it. ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾, that is, do not accept their words even if they present them as sincere advice. By "the disbelievers" is meant those who openly display disbelief, and by "the hypocrites" those who display Islam and conceal disbelief. It is narrated that "the disbelievers" here refers to Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and "the hypocrites" here to Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, though the general sense is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 4:

﴿God has not made for any man two hearts within his body.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: There was a man among Quraysh who was called Dhu l-Qalbayn (the Possessor of Two Hearts) because of the intensity of his understanding, so the verse was revealed to negate that. It was also said: this expression came as a preface (tawtiʾah) to the negation that follows it, meaning: just as God has not made for any man two hearts within his body, so He has not made your wives your mothers, nor your adopted sons your sons. ﴿Those of your wives with whom you make zihar (unlawful comparison to your mother's back)﴾: that is, you say to a wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." The Arabs used this expression to mean prohibition, and its ruling comes in Surat al-Mujadilah. The verb was followed by min (from) because it implies the meaning of "they keep away from them." ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾: al-adʿiyaʾ is the plural of daʿiy, which is one who is claimed as the son of someone while he is not his son. The occasion of its revelation was the matter of Zayd ibn Harithah: he was a young man from the tribe of Kalb, and some of the Arabs captured him and sold him to Khadijah, and she gave him to the Prophet ﷺ, who adopted him; so he was called Zayd ibn Muhammad until this verse was revealed. ﴿That is your saying﴾: the reference is to attributing the adopted son to other than his father, or to all of the negated matters mentioned above. His words ﴿with your mouths﴾ emphasize the falsity of the statement.
"Call them by their fathers' names" — the pronoun refers to the adopted sons (al-adi'a'), meaning: attribute them to their biological fathers, the ones who begot them.

The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves (33:6). This implies that they should love him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, more than they love themselves, and that they should support his religion more than they support themselves. "And his wives are their mothers": God has given the wives of the Prophet ﷺ the sanctity of mothers, in that marrying them is forbidden and it is obligatory to honour them, but He has made it obligatory to veil them from men.

"And those of blood-relationship are closer to one another" (33:6): this abrogates what was in the early days of Islam regarding inheritance through the brotherhood of Islam and through emigration (hijrah), and we have discussed this in the commentary on Surat al-Anfal.

"In the Book of God" (33:6): it may mean the Qur'an, or the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz).

"Of the believers" (33:6): it may be an explanation of "those of blood-relationship," or it may be connected to "closer" (awla), meaning: those of blood-relationship are closer in inheritance than the believers who are not related by blood.

"Except that you do a kindness to your allies" (33:6): this means doing good to the allies who are not kin, and benefiting them during their lifetime and making a bequest to them at death. That is permissible and recommended even if they are not relatives, but inheritance is for kin specifically. There is a difference of opinion as to whether "allies" here refers specifically to believers, or to both believers and unbelievers.

"Written in the Book" (33:6): meaning the Qur'an or the Preserved Tablet.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 7:

﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ It is the covenant to convey the message and to uphold the laws (shara'i') of the faith. It was also said: it is the covenant which He took when He brought forth the children of Adam from the loins of Adam like particles (dharr). The first view is more preponderant, because it is the one specific to the prophets. ﴿And [especially] from you, and from Noah﴾ These were already included in the category of the prophets, but He singled them out for mention to honour them, and He placed Muhammad ﷺ first to show his superiority. ﴿a solemn covenant﴾ means the covenant mentioned above. He repeated it for emphasis, and to describe it as "solemn" (ghalitha), that is, firm and established, such that it must be fulfilled.

﴿That He may question the truthful﴾. The *lam* here may be the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*), or the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-sayrura*, the *lam* indicating an outcome rather than an intention). The truthfulness (*al-sidq*) here may refer to truthfulness in speech, or truthfulness in deeds and resolve. It may also be that by "the truthful" (*al-sadiqin*) he means the prophets and the other believers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 9:

﴿Remember the favour of God upon you when hosts came against you﴾ This verse and what follows were revealed concerning the episode of the Battle of the Trench (ghazwat al-Khandaq). The hosts mentioned are the Quraysh and those of the disbelievers who were with them. God named them in this surah the "Confederates" (al-Ahzab), and they numbered about ten thousand. They besieged the city, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) dug a trench around it, to prevent them from entering it. ﴿So We sent against them a wind﴾ God sent against them the east wind (rih al-Saba), which extinguished their fires and overturned their cooking pots, and they could not remain in place because of it, so they departed defeated. ﴿And hosts you did not see﴾ meaning the angels.

When they came upon you from above you and from below you (﴿إِذْ جَآءُوكُمْ مِّن فَوْقِكُمْ وَمِنْ أَسْفَلَ مِنكُمْ﴾). That is, they besieged the city from its upper part and from its lower part. It was also said that "from above you" refers to the people of Najd, since their land lies above Medina, and "from below you" refers to the people of Makkah and the rest of Tihamah.

﴿And when the eyes shifted (from their places)﴾ (﴿وَإِذْ زَاغَتِ ٱلأَبْصَارُ﴾): that is, they turned away from their positions, and this is an expression for intense fear.

﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ (﴿وَبَلَغَتِ ٱلْقُلُوبُ ٱلْحَنَاجِرَ﴾). "Hanajir" is the plural of "hanjarah," which is the gullet (throat). The arrival of the heart at the throat is a metaphor (majaz), an expression for intense fear. It was also said that it is literal (haqiqah), because the lungs swell from intense fear, so they rise, and the heart rises with their rising to the throat.

﴿And you harboured thoughts about Allah, (various) thoughts﴾ (﴿وَتَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ ٱلظُّنُونَاْ﴾). That is, you thought that the disbelievers would overpower you, although Allah had promised you victory over them. As for the hypocrites, they harboured an evil assumption and openly declared it. As for the believers, a passing thought may have occurred to some of them of a kind that humans cannot repel; then they regained insight and put their trust in Allah's promise.

Nafi' read "al-Dhununa," "al-Rasula," and "al-Sabila" with an alif both in pause and in continuity. Another reading omits it in continuity but keeps it in pause. Abu 'Amr and Hamzah omitted it in pause but not in continuity. As for omitting it, that is the original form; as for retaining it, it is to balance the verse-endings (ra'us al-ayy), since they are like rhyming final syllables (qawafi). This reason requires that it be retained in pause specifically. As for those who retained it in both states, they treated continuity as if it were pause.

Here is the translation of the passage:

﴿There, the believers were tested﴾, that is, they were put to the test or afflicted with trial. The element governing the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) is "was tested" (ibtulliya). It has also been said that it is what precedes it. ﴿And they were shaken violently﴾. The root meaning of zalzalah (violent shaking, the term for an earthquake) is intense agitation, and here it is an expression for the disturbance of hearts.
﴿And when the hypocrites say﴾ ﴿And when the hypocrites say﴾ It is related that he was Mu'attib ibn Qushayr.

"And when a group among them said, 'O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you [to stand], so return.' And a faction of them sought permission from the Prophet, saying, 'Indeed, our houses are exposed,' [when] they were not exposed; they only wished to flee."

Wait, that is not what I was given. Here is the faithful translation of the passage as it stands:

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 33, verse 13:

﴿And when a group among them said﴾ Al-Suhayli said: "al-ta'ifah (the group) applies to one person or more." The intended one here is Aws ibn Qayzi. ﴿O people of Yathrib, there is no station for you, so return.﴾ Yathrib is the name of the city, and it was said: it is the name of the district at one side of which the city lies. Maqam (station) is the name of a place from qiyam (standing), i.e., there is no standing for you here, meaning the place of fighting. It was also read with a ḍammah (muqam), and that is the name of a place from iqamah (residing), i.e., there is no residence for you here. Their saying "so return" means, return to your dwellings in Medina and leave off fighting. ﴿And a faction of them asks permission of the Prophet﴾ meaning they asked him for permission to depart. The one asking permission was Aws ibn Qayzi and his clan; it was also said: Banu Haritha. ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾ meaning exposed to the enemy. It was also said: empty for thieves. So God declared them liars in that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 14:

﴿And if it had been entered upon them from its surrounding areas﴾ That is, if the city had been entered upon them from its sides. ﴿Then they had been asked for strife﴾ By strife (fitnah) he means disbelief or fighting against the Muslims. ﴿They would have come to it﴾ With the short vowel (al-qasr), اتَوْهَا (*atawhā*) means they came to it. With the long vowel (al-madd), أَتَوْهَا (*ātawhā*) means they gave it from themselves. ﴿And they would not have lingered therein﴾ The pronoun refers to the city.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 18:

﴿Allah already knows﴾ "Qad" (indeed/already) has entered upon the present-tense verb here with the sense of a warning (tahdid). It has also been said that it is for causal explanation (ta'lil) in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum). ﴿those who hinder among you﴾ That is, those who hinder people from jihad and prevent them from it by their words and actions. ﴿and those who say to their brothers, "Come here to us"﴾ They are the hypocrites who stayed behind in Madinah from jihad, and they would say to their kinsmen, or to those like them among the hypocrites: "Come to sit with us in Madinah and abandon fighting." Hallumma (come here) has already been mentioned in al-An'am [150].

﴿And they do not come to the battle except a little﴾ Al-ba's means fighting. "Qaleelan" (a little) is an adjective for a verb-noun (masdar) that has been omitted, its estimated form being: "except a little coming." Or it is an exception from the subject of "ya'tuna" (they come): that is, except a few of them.

﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ *(grudging towards you)*. أشحة (*ashiḥḥah*) is the plural of شحيح (*shaḥīḥ*), on the pattern فعيل (*fa'īl*). Its meaning is that they are stingy with themselves, so they do not fight. It was also said that they are stingy with their wealth. And it was said that the meaning is "grudging towards you at the time of war," that is, they are anxious lest they be killed. أشحة is in the accusative (نصب) as a circumstantial qualifier (حال) of the subject of the speakers (القائلين), or of those who obstruct (المعوقين), or of the pronoun in يأتون (*ya'tūn*, "they come"). Or it is in the accusative of censure (على الذم).

﴿فَإِذَا جَآءَ ٱلْخَوْفُ رَأَيْتَهُمْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ﴾ *(So when fear comes, you see them looking at you)*, that is, when the fear of the enemies intensifies, these people look at you in that state and seek refuge in you because of the intensity of their fear. ﴿تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ كَٱلَّذِي يُغْشَىٰ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْمَوْتِ﴾ *(their eyes roll like one who faints from the approach of death)*, an expression of the intensity of their fear.

﴿فَإِذَا ذَهَبَ ٱلْخَوْفُ سَلَقُوكُمْ بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ﴾ *(But when fear departs, they assail you with sharp tongues)*. السلق (*salq*) with the tongues is an expression for speaking with harsh, offensive speech. حداد (*ḥidād*) means eloquent people able to speak. When God grants you victory and fear departs, the hypocrites return to harming you with abuse and belittling of the Sharia. It was also said: when you gain spoils, they demand a share of the spoils.

﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَى ٱلْخَيْرِ﴾ *(grudging towards good)*, that is, they are stingy in doing good. It was also said: they are stingy with the spoils. Its accusative case here is a circumstantial qualifier (حال) of the agent in سلقوكم (*salaqūkum*, "they assail you").

﴿لَمْ يُؤْمِنُواْ فَأَحْبَطَ ٱللَّهُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾ *(They did not believe, so God nullified their deeds)*. The meaning is not that the deeds were nullified after having been established. Rather, the meaning is that they were not accepted, because faith is a condition for the acceptance of deeds. It was also said that they became hypocrites after having believed, so on this view the nullification (إحباط, *ihbāṭ*) is literal.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 20:

﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾ The confederates (al-Ahzab) here are the disbelievers of Quraysh and those with them. The meaning is that the hypocrites, out of their extreme dread, think the confederates have not departed from Madinah, when in fact they have departed. ﴿And if the confederates should come, they would wish they were in the desert among the Bedouins﴾ Yawaddu (يَوَدُّواْ) means they wish (yatamanna). Badun (بَادُونَ) means those who go out into the desert (al-badiyah), and al-A'rab (الأعراب) are the people of the desert among the Arabs. The meaning of the verse is: if the confederates were to come to Madinah again, these hypocrites, out of their extreme dread, would wish to be in the desert with the Bedouins, and not to be in Madinah but absent from it, asking those who arrive among them about your news.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 21:

﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾ meaning: a model for you to follow him (ﷺ) in certainty, patience, and all other virtues. It is also recited as "uswah" with the first letter (hamza) vowelled with a damma, and the meaning is the same.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 22:

﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾. It has been said: this promise is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed them of when he ordered the digging of the trench (khandaq), namely that the disbelievers would descend upon them and then they would turn away disappointed. It has also been said: it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed on before you? Adversity and hardship touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], and so on, and they knew that they would be tested and then granted victory.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 23:

﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to God.﴾ Meaning: he was killed as a martyr (shahid). Anas ibn Malik said: it refers to my uncle Anas ibn al-Nadr. It was also said: it refers to Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib. Qada' al-nahb (fulfilling one's vow) is an expression for death, according to Ibn Abbas and others. It was also said: qada nahbahu means he fulfilled the covenant he made with God. This is supported by what is related, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "Talhah is among those who have fulfilled their vow," and he had not been killed at that time. ﴿And among them are those who wait﴾: the object is omitted, i.e., they wait to fulfill their vow, or they wait for martyrdom in the way of God according to Ibn Abbas's view, or they wait to attain the highest ranks of faith and righteousness according to the other view.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 26:

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who supported them from their fortresses﴾ The sayasi (ṣayāṣī) are the fortresses. The verse was revealed concerning the Jews of Banu Qurayza. They had been under covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke his covenant and sided with Quraysh. When Quraysh withdrew from Madina, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged Banu Qurayza until they agreed to submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh; he ruled that their men be killed, and their women and children be taken captive. ﴿A group you killed﴾ meaning the men, and that day there were killed from them every one who had reached puberty, and they were between eight hundred and nine hundred. ﴿And you took captive a group﴾ meaning the women and children.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 27:

﴿And He caused you to inherit their land﴾, meaning the land of Banu Qurayza, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided among the Muhajirun. ﴿And land you had not yet trodden﴾: this is a promise of conquering lands that the Muslims had not yet set foot in at that time, namely Makkah, Yemen, al-Sham, Iraq and Egypt. Allah thus caused the Muslims to inherit all of that and what lies beyond it, as far as the farthest east and west. However, it is my view that it may also mean the land of Banu Qurayza, because He said "caused you to inherit" in the past tense, and that was the land they had taken at that time, whereas other lands were taken only after that. Had He meant those, He would have said "will cause you to inherit." He repeated it with the conjunction to describe it by His words "that you had not yet trodden," i.e., you had not entered it before that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 28:

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: "If you desire the life of this world and its adornment..."﴾ etc. Its occasion (sabab) was that the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were jealous of one another, to the point that this distressed him. It is also said that they asked him for clothing and large expenses. His wives at that time were nine women: five from Quraysh, namely: ʿĀʾishah bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ḥafṣah bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭab, may Allah be pleased with him, Sawdah bint Zamʿah, Umm Ḥabībah bint Abi Sufyan, and Umm Salamah bint Abi Umayyah al-Makhzumi; and four from outside Quraysh, namely: Maymunah bint al-Ḥarith al-Hilaliyyah, Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy from the Children of Israel, Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyyah, and Juwayriyyah bint al-Ḥarith from the Banu al-Mustaliq. ﴿So come, I will provide for you and release you in a graceful release.﴾ The original meaning of taʿāla (come) is that one who is in a high place says it to one who is in a low place; then it came to be used in the sense of "approach" in all places. ﴿Umatticʿkunna﴾ (I will provide for you) is from al-mutʿah (provision), which is kindness shown to a woman when she is divorced, and al-sarāḥ (release) is divorce. So the meaning of the verse is: Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to give his wives the choice between divorce with provision, if they desired the adornment of this world, and remaining in his marriage, if they desired the Hereafter. He (ﷺ) began with ʿĀʾishah, and she chose to remain in his marriage; then the rest of them followed her in that, so no divorce took place. ʿĀʾishah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave us the choice, and we chose him, and that was not counted as a divorce." And if the one given the choice chooses divorce: the school of Mālik holds that it is three (talaqs). It is also said: one irrevocable divorce; and it is said: one revocable divorce. As for describing the release as "graceful" (jamīl): it may mean that it is less than three, or it may mean that it is three; and its beauty lies in good treatment, generosity, and keeping the covenant.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 29:

﴿For the good-doers among you﴾ "Min" here is explanatory (li-l-bayan), not partitive (li-l-tab'id), because all of them are good-doers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 30:

﴿بِفَاحِشَةٍ مُّبَيِّنَةٍ﴾ It is said: this means fornication (al-zina). It is also said: it means disobedience toward their husband, peace be upon him (ﷺ), or imposing upon him what burdens him. It is also said: it is a general term covering all sins. ﴿يُضَاعَفْ لَهَا ٱلْعَذَابُ ضِعْفَيْنِ﴾ That is, her punishment in the Hereafter will be twice the punishment of others. This is because of the elevated rank of these women, since everyone is held accountable according to his or her station. Abu 'Amr recited "yuda''af" with the ya' and the raf' of "al-'adhab," in the passive form (al-bina' lil-maf'ul). Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir recited "nudha''if" with the nun and the nasb of "al-'adhab," in the active form (al-bina' lil-fa'il).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 31:

﴿Whoever of you is devoutly obedient to Allah and His Messenger﴾ It is read with the ya' (yaqnut), taking the form of the word "man" (whoever) into account, and with the ta' (taqnut), taking its meaning into account. The same applies to "ta'mal" (does [good]). Qunut here means obedience. ﴿We will give her, her reward twice over﴾ meaning her rewards for good deeds will be doubled. ﴿and We have prepared for her a generous provision﴾ meaning Paradise. It was also said that it means provision in this world, but the first view is the correct one.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 32:

﴿You are not like anyone among the women, if you fear Allah.﴾ Allah has preferred them over the women on condition of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety), and taqwa was realized in them, so the preference over all women was realized. However, this generality excludes Fatimah, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Maryam bint Imran, and Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, because of the testimony of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that each of them is "the chief of the women of her world." ﴿So do not be soft in speech﴾ He forbade speech that is soft and pleasing to men, which inclines them towards women. ﴿lest one in whose heart is a disease should covet﴾ That is, immorality and inclination towards women. It has been said that it means hypocrisy (nifaq), but this is far-fetched in this context. ﴿but speak a known word﴾ That is, the correct speech, or speech free of anything He has forbidden.

﴿And abide in your houses﴾ is read with a kasra on the qaf (قرئ بكسر القاف), and it allows two possibilities. It may derive from *al-waqar* (dignity, gravity), or from *al-qarar* (remaining in a place). In that case the first *ra'* was dropped, as the *lam* was dropped in ظلت (*ẓalt*). As for the reading with a fatha, it derives from *al-qarar* (remaining in a place), following the dialect of those who say قررت (*qararta*) with a kasra for the present يقر (*yaqirru*) with a fatha. The well-known usage in the language is the reverse of this. It was also said that it derives from قار يقار (*qara yaqaru*), meaning "to gather." The meaning of *qarar* is more preferred, because Sawda, may God be pleased with her, was asked, "Why do you not go out?" She replied, "God has commanded us to remain in our houses." 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, would weep whenever she recited this verse, regretting her going out on the day of the Camel. At that time, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said to her, "Indeed God has commanded you to remain in your house."

﴿And do not display yourselves as was the display of the former Jahiliyya﴾. Tabarruj (display) means showing one's adornment. ﴿The display of the former Jahiliyya﴾, that is, like what the women of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) used to do, namely exposing themselves and presenting themselves to be looked at. He described it as "former" in comparison with the state of Islam. It was also said that "the former Jahiliyya" refers to the period between Adam and Noah, and it was said to be the period between Moses and Jesus.

﴿Uncleanness﴾ (الرِّجْسَ, *ar-rijs*) originally means impurity, and what is meant by it here is deficiencies and defects. ﴿O People of the House﴾ (أَهْلَ ٱلْبَيْتِ, *ahla al-bayt*) is either a vocative (*munada*) or an accusative of specification (*takhsis*, singling out). The People of the House of the Prophet (ﷺ) are his wives, his descendants, and his relatives, such as al-'Abbas and 'Ali, and everyone for whom charity (*sadaqa*) is forbidden. It was also said that what is meant here is his wives specifically, and "house" in this view means the dwelling. This view is weak, because the address uses the masculine form, and if he had meant that, it would have said عنكن (*'ankunna*, feminine plural). It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: this verse was revealed concerning five people: the children of 'Ali, Fatima, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 34:

﴿And remember﴾ is an address to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). He singled them out after their inclusion together with the People of the House. This remembrance may be either recitation or remembrance in the heart. "The signs of Allah" are the Qur'an, and "the wisdom" is the Sunnah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 35:

﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ etc. Its occasion of revelation: some women said, "Allah mentions the men and does not mention us," so the mention of women was revealed concerning them. ﴿and the believing men and believing women﴾. Islam (al-islam) is submission (al-inqiyad), and iman (al-iman) is affirmation (al-tasdiq). Then both are used in three ways according to difference of meaning, as in His saying: "You have not believed, but say: 'We have submitted'" [al-Hujurat: 14]; and in agreement when they are combined, as in His saying: ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 35], etc.; and in generality, so that Islam is more general, since it is by the heart and the limbs, while iman is more specific, since it is by the heart alone. This is the most apparent meaning in this context. ﴿and the devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women﴾ may mean worship (al-ibadah) or obedience (al-ta'ah). ﴿and the truthful men and truthful women﴾ may mean truthfulness of speech (sidq al-qawl) or truthfulness of resolve (sidq al-azm).

This is a commentary (tafsir) by Ibn Juzayy on Surah al-Ahzab (33), verse 36.

﴿And it is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affairs.﴾ The meaning is that neither a believing man nor a believing woman has any choice (ikhtiyar) in the presence of Allah and His Messenger. Rather, it is obligatory upon them to submit (taslim) and comply (inqiyad) with the command of Allah and His Messenger. The pronoun in His words "from their affair" (min amrihim) refers back to the plural that is implied by His words "for a believing man or a believing woman," because its meaning is general, encompassing all believing men and believing women. This verse serves as a preface (tawti'ah) to the story mentioned after it.

It has been said that its occasion of revelation (sabab) was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proposed marriage to a woman on behalf of his freedman (mawla), Zayd ibn Harithah, but she and her family disliked this. When the verse was revealed, they said: "We are pleased, O Messenger of Allah." It is disputed whether this woman who was proposed to was Zaynab bint Jahsh or someone else. It has also been said that she was Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 37:

﴿And when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favor and you had bestowed favor, "Keep your wife and fear Allah,"﴾ He is Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi. Allah's favor upon him was Islam and other things, and the Prophet's ﷺ favor was manumission. Zayd had as his wife Zaynab bint Jahsh, who was the daughter of Umaymah, the paternal aunt of the Prophet ﷺ. Zayd complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about her poor treatment of him and her arrogance toward him, and he wanted to divorce her. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: ﴿Keep your wife and fear Allah﴾, meaning regarding what he described her as having, of poor treatment: fear Allah and do not divorce her. This is a prohibition of divorce in the sense of disapproval, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The most hateful of permissible things to Allah is divorce."

﴿And you concealed within yourself that which Allah was to disclose﴾ What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concealed was a permissible matter, with no sin or blame in it. But he feared that Allah would give their tongues power over him and they would speak ill of him, so he concealed it out of modesty, decorum, and protection of his honor. It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was eager that Zayd divorce Zaynab so that he himself could marry her, because of her kinship to him and her nobility. He said: "Keep her, since she is your wife," while concealing his eagerness for her out of fear of people's speech, lest they say: he married the wife of his son, since he had adopted him. So what the Prophet ﷺ concealed was his desire to marry her, and Allah disclosed it by decreeing his marriage to her. Aisha said: "If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been concealing anything of the revelation, he would have concealed this verse, because of how harsh it was upon him." It is also said: Allah had revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he should marry Zaynab after Zayd's divorce, so what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concealed was what Allah had informed him of concerning that.

﴿So when Zayd had no further need of her, We married her to you﴾ None of the Companions is mentioned by name in the Qur'an except Zayd ibn Harithah. Al-Wattar (the need) means need, i.e., when Zayd no longer had any need for her, Allah married her to His Prophet ﷺ. Allah attributed the marriage to Himself to honor her. For this reason Zaynab used to boast over the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and say: "Allah married me to His Prophet from above the seven heavens." Some scholars used His words "We married her to you" as evidence that in the marriage contract it is better to say "he married her to him" (ankahahu iyyaha), putting the husband's pronoun before the wife's pronoun, as in the verse ﴿So that there will be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾. The meaning is that Allah married Zaynab, the wife of Zayd, to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to make known to the believers that marrying the wives of their adopted sons is lawful for them, since adopted sons are not truly their sons.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 38:

﴿There is no restriction upon the Prophet in what Allah has ordained for him﴾. The meaning is that the Prophet's ﷺ marriage to Zaynab after Zayd is lawful; there is no sin in it, no blame, and no reproach. In this there is a refutation of those among the hypocrites who spoke about this matter. Here "fard" (ordained) means "qasama" (apportioned) for him. ﴿The way of Allah with those who passed away before, and the command of Allah is a decree determined﴾, that is, it is Allah's custom with the earlier Prophets that they attain what Allah has made lawful for them. It has also been said that the reference in this is to Dawud (David) and his marriage to the woman concerning which what happened to him happened, but the general meaning is better. The word "sunnah" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), or by implying a verb, or as a warning (al-igra').

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah al-Ahzab, verse 39:

﴿ٱلَّذِينَ يُبَلِّغُونَ رِسَالاَتِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("Those who convey the messages of Allah") is a description (ṣifah) of "those who passed away before" (alladhīna khalaw min qabl), and they are the prophets. Alternatively, it is in the nominative (rafʿ) by an implied subject (mubtadaʾ), or in the accusative (naṣb) by an implied verb.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 40:

﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men﴾ This is a refutation of those who said of Zayd ibn Harithah, "Zayd ibn Muhammad," and objected to the Prophet ﷺ marrying Zayd's wife. The generality of the negation in the verse is not contradicted by the existence of al-Hasan and al-Husayn, because he ﷺ was not their father in reality, since they were not from his loins; rather, they were the sons of his daughter. As for his male offspring, they died young, so they are not among the men. ﴿But he is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets﴾ That is, the last of them, so there is no prophet after him ﷺ. It has also been read with a kasra on the ta' (khatim), meaning that he sealed them, so he is the seal; and with a fatha, meaning that they were sealed by him, so he is like the signet and stamp for them. If it is said: Jesus will descend at the end of time, and so he will come after the Prophet ﷺ, the answer is that prophethood was given to Jesus before him ﷺ. Moreover, when Jesus descends, he will do so under the law of the Prophet ﷺ, so he is as if he were one of his community.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah al-Ahzab, verses 41–42:

﴿Remember Allah with much remembrance﴾. Allah has stipulated abundance in remembrance wherever He has commanded it, unlike other acts of worship. Remembrance (dhikr) may be by the heart and by the tongue, and it takes many forms: tahlil (saying "there is no god but Allah"), tasbih (saying "Glory be to Allah"), hamd (saying "Praise be to Allah"), takbir (saying "Allah is greatest"), and mentioning the names of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And glorify Him morning and evening﴾. It has been said that this refers to the Fajr and 'Asr prayers. The more apparent view is that He commanded tasbih at the beginning of the day and at its end. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He meant at all times, for the limits of the day are its two extremities.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah al-Ahzab, verses 41–42:

﴿Remember Allah with much remembrance﴾. Allah has stipulated abundance in remembrance wherever He has commanded it, unlike other acts of worship. Remembrance (dhikr) may be by the heart and by the tongue, and it takes many forms: tahlil (saying "there is no god but Allah"), tasbih (saying "Glory be to Allah"), hamd (saying "Praise be to Allah"), takbir (saying "Allah is greatest"), and mentioning the names of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And glorify Him morning and evening﴾. It has been said that this refers to the Fajr and 'Asr prayers. The more apparent view is that He commanded tasbih at the beginning of the day and at its end. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He meant at all times, for the limits of the day are its two extremities.

He it is who showers blessings upon you, and His angels (do so too), that He may bring you out (﴿هُوَ ٱلَّذِي يُصَلِّي عَلَيْكُمْ وَمَلاَئِكَتُهُ لِيُخْرِجَكُمْ﴾). This is an address to the believers. The blessing (ṣalāh) of Allah upon them is mercy towards them, and the blessing of the angels upon them is their supplication for them. So the word yuṣallī is used in both senses, although they differ. It has also been said that it is elliptical, with an omitted noun, and its meaning is: "and His angels pray (yuṣallūn)."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 44:

﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be, "Peace."﴿ "It is said: it means the Day of Resurrection. And it is said: it means in Paradise, and this is the more preferred view, because of His saying: ﴿And their greeting therein will be, "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. It is possible that He means their greeting one another with peace, or the words of the angels to them: ﴿"Peace be upon you; you have done well"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]."

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verses 45–46:**

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾, i.e., he bears witness over his community. ﴿and a bringer of good news and a warner﴾, ﴿and one who invites to Allah by His permission﴾, i.e., by the command of Allah and His sending. ﴿and as an illuminating lamp﴾, a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for the light that the religion contains.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verses 45–46:**

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾, i.e., he bears witness over his community. ﴿and a bringer of good news and a warner﴾, ﴿and one who invites to Allah by His permission﴾, i.e., by the command of Allah and His sending. ﴿and as an illuminating lamp﴾, a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for the light that the religion contains.

﴿And disregard their harm﴾ admits of two meanings. The first is: do not harm them. On this reading, the verbal noun (al-masdar) is annexed to its object. According to this interpretation, the part of the verse concerning the disbelievers was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

The second meaning is: bear their harm to you, and turn away from their statements. On this reading, the verbal noun is annexed to its agent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 49:

﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them﴾ etc. Its meaning is the removal of the waiting period (ʿiddah) from a divorced woman before consummation. Thus "nikah" (marriage) in the verse means the contract (ʿaqd), and "touching" (massa) means intercourse (jimaʿ), and "you count them" means you reckon their waiting period (ʿiddah) for them. ﴿Then provide for them⟩ This requires that a woman divorced before consummation be given a provision (mutʿah), whether a bridal gift (faridah, sadaq) has been fixed for her or not. And the Almighty's saying in al-Baqarah [2:237]: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified for them an obligation, then give half of what you have specified⟩ requires that a woman divorced before consummation for whom a bridal gift has been fixed is owed half the bridal gift, and has no provision (mutʿah). Scholars have differed over whether this verse abrogates the verse of al-Baqarah or is abrogated by it. It is possible to reconcile the two, by taking the verse of al-Baqarah as clarifying this one and specifying its general application.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 50:

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives whom you have given their bridal payments (ujur)﴾. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first is that what is meant is his wives who were under his marriage at that time, such as ʿAisha and others, and he had given them their dowries (mahr). The second is that what is meant is all women, so Allah permitted him to marry any woman to whom he gives her dowry, and this is broader than the first. ﴿And what your right hand possesses﴾: Allah permitted him, along with the wives, concubines by right of ownership (milk al-yamin). By His saying ﴿what Allah has returned to you﴾ He means the spoils of war (ghana'im). ﴿And the daughters of your paternal uncles, and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts﴾: He means his relatives from his father's side and from his mother's side. The Prophet ﷺ had paternal uncles and paternal aunts, being the brothers and sisters of his father, but he had no maternal brother or sister. By his maternal uncles and maternal aunts is meant only the kin of his mother, who were the Banu Zuhra, and for this reason they used to say, "We are the maternal uncles of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." So whoever says that what is meant by His saying ﴿We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ is those who were under his marriage, then the following is a conjunction to them, and a permission to marry his relatives in addition to those who were under his marriage. And whoever says that what is meant is all women, then it is a singling out of them in a manner of honour, after these (relatives) have entered into the generality. ﴿Those who emigrated with you﴾: a specification by which he guards against those who did not emigrate, such as the "freed ones" (tulaqa') who embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾: Allah permitted the Prophet ﷺ to take any of the women who gave themselves to him. It is disputed whether this actually occurred or not. Ibn ʿAbbas said: no woman was with the Prophet ﷺ except by marriage or by right of ownership, not by a woman giving herself in gift; and the recitation of the majority supports this, ﴿in tawahhabat﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, meaning "if it occurs." It was also said: this has occurred, and according to this opinion it was recited ﴿an wahabat﴾ with a fatha on the hamza. According to this opinion it is disputed who it was who gave herself in gift: it was said Maymuna bint al-Harith, it was said Zaynab bint Khuzayma Umm al-Masakin, it was said Umm Sharik al-Ansariyya, and it was said Umm Sharik al-ʿAmiriyya.

﴿Exclusively for you, to the exclusion of the believers﴾: that is, a woman giving herself in gift is a special privilege for the Prophet ﷺ alone, not for anyone else. Observe how he turned from the third person (absence) to the second person (address) so as to single out the one addressed alone. It was also said: "exclusively" (khalisa) refers to everything mentioned before, namely the women lawful to him ﷺ, because the rest of the believers were restricted to four wives, whereas he ﷺ was permitted more than that. The position of Malik is that a marriage contracted with the wording of a gift is not valid, in contrast to Abu Hanifa. As for its i'rab (grammatical analysis): ﴿khalisa﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar), or a circumstantial state (hal), or an adjective (sifa) of "woman". ﴿We have indeed known what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives﴾: meaning the rulings of marriage, such as the bridal payment, the guardian (wali), restriction to four, and other matters. ﴿So that there is no difficulty for you﴾: it is connected to the verse before it, that is: We have explained the rulings of marriage so that there be no difficulty for you, or so that it not be thought of you that you did what is not permitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to His saying ﴿exclusively for you﴾.

The meaning of ﴿turjī﴾ is "you delay and put aside," and the meaning of ﴿tu'wī﴾ is "you take in and draw near." There is disagreement over what is meant by this postponing and taking in. It was said that it concerns the division of time among them: you may give more to whomever you wish and less to whomever you wish. It was also said that it concerns divorce: you keep whomever you wish and divorce whomever you wish. And it was said that it means you marry whomever you wish and leave whomever you wish. On every view, the meaning is a widening of latitude for the Prophet ﷺ, and a permission for him to do what he wills. The transmitters agree that he ﷺ was just in dividing his time among his wives, taking this as the best of character, while God had granted him permission otherwise. As for the pronoun in His words ﴿minhunna﴾ ("of them"), it refers either to his wives ﷺ specifically, or to all that God made lawful for him, according to the earlier disagreement.

﴿And whomever you seek out from those you have set aside, there is no blame upon you﴾. Regarding its meaning there are two views. One is: whomever you had set aside from your wives, there is no blame on you in taking her back after setting her aside. The other is: whomever you seek and whomever you set aside are alike in being permitted. Thus "min" is partitive on the first view, while on the second view it is like your saying: "whoever meets you and whoever does not meet you is the same."

﴿That is nearer to their eyes being cooled﴾: meaning, when they know that this is the command of God, their eyes are cooled by it and they are content with it, and the jealousy that was among them is removed. For the occasion of revelation of this verse was the jealousy that arose among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, some of them toward others.

"﴿There are no more women lawful to you after this﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: no women are lawful to you other than those who are in your marriage now, and you may not add to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them the choice and they chose Allah and His Messenger, Allah rewarded them for that by forbidding other women to him, as an honour to them. The second opinion: no women are lawful to you other than the categories that were named. The disagreement here follows the disagreement over the meaning of His words: ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾, meaning: no one other than those mentioned is lawful to you, as was stated earlier. It was also said that the meaning of "no women are lawful to you" is: Jewish and Christian women are not lawful to you after the believing women mentioned; but this is far-fetched.

Scholars differed about the ruling of this verse. It was said that it is abrogated (mansukh) by His words ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾, on the view that the intended meaning is all women. It was also said that this verse abrogates that one (i.e., the earlier verse), on the view that the intended meaning is those who were in his marriage; and this is the more apparent view, for the reason we mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, and because the nine wives in his case (peace be upon him) are like the four wives in the case of his community.

﴿Nor that you should exchange them for other wives﴾: its meaning is that it is not lawful for you to divorce any one of them and marry another in her place.

﴿Even though their beauty pleases you﴾: in this there is evidence for the permissibility of looking at a woman when a man wishes to marry her.

﴿Except what your right hand possesses﴾: the meaning is that Allah permitted him to have slave-women (ima', sing. amah, female bondservants). The exception is either in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for "women," or in the accusative position as an exception from the pronoun in "their beauty."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 53:

﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you for a meal﴾. The occasion of this verse is what Anas narrated: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married Zaynab bint Jahsh, he held a wedding feast (walima) for her and invited the people. When they had eaten, a group remained seated in a part of the house, and this burdened the Prophet ﷺ, so he went out so that they would leave with his departure. He passed by the chambers of his wives, then returned and found them still in their place, so he departed, and they left at that. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was revealed concerning people who would watch for the Prophet's ﷺ meal, entering upon him before the food and sitting until it was cooked, then eating and not leaving. So they were commanded not to enter until they were given permission, and to depart once they had eaten. I say: the first account is more well-known, while Ibn ʿAbbas's account is more fitting with what the verse contains of the prohibition of entering until permission is given. So, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, the prohibition on entering until permission is given, and according to the first account, the prohibition on remaining seated after eating, for the verse includes both rulings. ﴿Not waiting for its time﴾, i.e., not waiting for the time of the food. The word ināʾ means the time, and it was said: ināʾ is the cooking and ripening of the food, from the saying anā yaʾnī inā'an. ﴿But when you are invited, then enter﴾: a command to enter after the invitation, and in this there is emphasis on the prohibition of entering before it. ﴿And when you have eaten, then disperse﴾: i.e., leave. Some of them said: this is a manner which Allah taught to those who overstay. ﴿Nor lingering for conversation﴾: it is coordinated with "not waiting," or its implied sense is: "and do not enter lingering." Its meaning is the prohibition against seeking to sit for the enjoyment of conversation with one another, or seeking to listen to the talk of the people of the household; and their "istiʾnās" is eavesdropping and spying. ﴿Indeed, that was troubling the Prophet﴾: meaning their sitting for conversation or their entering without permission. ﴿And he is shy of you﴾: its implied sense is that he is shy of expelling you, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿But Allah is not shy of the truth﴾: i.e., that your expulsion is a truth which Allah does not abandon.

﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen﴾. Matāʿ means the need, among furnishings and other things. This verse was revealed concerning the veiling of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and its occasion was what Anas narrated about the people sitting in Zaynab's house on the day of the feast. It was also said: its occasion was that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab suggested to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he screen his wives, so the verse was revealed in agreement with ʿUmar's statement. Some of them said: when this verse was revealed concerning the Mothers of the Believers, ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen﴾, it was not permissible for people to speak with them except from behind a screen, and it was not permissible for anyone to see them, whether veiled or unveiled; thus they were singled out with this over all other women. ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾: meaning, more pure from the thoughts that occur to men regarding women and women regarding men. ﴿Nor that you marry his wives﴾: its occasion was that some people said: if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dies, I will marry ʿAʾisha. So Allah forbade people to marry his wives after him, as an honour to him ﷺ.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 55:

﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers, nor their sons﴾ etc.: When Allah made the hijab obligatory, He permitted them to appear before their mahrams (those relatives whom they may never marry), who are: the fathers, the sons, the brothers, their sons, and the sons of their sisters. ﴿Nor their women﴾. It has been said that by "women" is meant the female relatives and those who serve them (al-musarrifat lahunna). It has also been said that it means the women of all believing women. The first view is strengthened by the restriction of "women" through the possessive pronoun ("their women"), and the second is strengthened by the fact that they did not veil themselves from women in general. ﴿Nor those whom their right hands possess﴾. Scholars differed regarding who, among those owned by the right hand (ma malakat aymanuhunna, i.e., slaves), they were permitted to appear before. It was said: only female slaves (al-ima') and not male slaves (al-abid). It was also said: both female and male slaves, and this is more fitting to the wording of the verse. Then those who held this view differed. Some said: only the male slaves owned by them, not those owned by others. This is the apparent meaning of the wording of the verse. Others said: all male slaves, whether they were in their own ownership or in the ownership of others.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet.﴾ This verse is an honour bestowed upon the Prophet ﷺ. We have already explained the meaning of the blessing of Allah and the blessing of the angels in His words ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels [too]﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43]. ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with the greeting of peace﴾. Sending blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ is an obligation of Islam, so the command to do so is taken to be obligatory, and at minimum it is to be done once in one's lifetime. As for its ruling within the prayer: the position of al-Shafi'i (Shafi'i school) is that it is an obligatory pillar, and the prayer is invalidated by omitting it; the position of Malik (Maliki school) is that it is a sunnah. Its form is what is recorded in the sound hadith: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious." The narrations on this differ greatly. As for greeting the Prophet ﷺ with peace, it may mean greeting him with peace in the tashahhud of the prayer, or greeting him at the time of meeting him. As for greeting him with peace after his death, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever greets me with peace from nearby, I hear him, and whoever greets me with peace from afar, it is conveyed to me. Indeed, Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the Prophets."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 57:

﴿Indeed, those who abuse Allah and His Messenger﴾ The abuse (idhayah) of Allah consists in associating partners with Him and attributing to Him a spouse and a son. The meaning of His being abused is not that harm reaches Him, for Exalted is He, nothing harms Him and nothing benefits Him. It has been said that the verse contains an elision (hadhf mudaf), its intended meaning being: "those who abuse the friends (awliya') of Allah." But the first interpretation is more preferred (arjah), because a hadith has been narrated in which Allah, Exalted is He, says: "The son of Adam abuses Me, and he has no right to abuse Me; he denies Me, and he has no right to deny Me. As for his abuse of Me, it is his saying: 'Allah has a spouse and a son.' As for his denial of Me, it is his saying: 'He will not restore me as He originated me.'" As for the abuse of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is confronting him with what he dislikes, whether by words or by deeds. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning those who slandered him when he took Safiyyah bint Huyayy.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 58:

﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾ [etc.]: This refers to slander (buhtan (false accusation)), which is mentioning a person with what is not in him. It is worse than backbiting (ghiba (speaking ill of someone in their absence)), even though backbiting is forbidden, and it is mentioning what is in a person of what he dislikes.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 59:

﴿O Prophet, tell your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers to draw their outer garments close around them.﴾ The women of the Arabs used to uncover their faces as slave women do, and this was an invitation for men to look at them. So God commanded them to draw down their outer garments (al-jalabib) so that they would cover their faces by this means. It is understood from this the difference between free women and slave women. Al-jalabib is the plural of jilbab, which is a garment larger than the khimar. It was said: it is the rida'  (a wrap or mantle). The manner of drawing it down, according to Ibn 'Abbas, is that she wraps it over her face until nothing shows of her except one eye with which she sees. It was also said: that she wraps it until only her eyes show. And it was said: that she covers half of her face. ﴿That is more suitable that they may be known and not be harmed.﴾ That is, this is closer to distinguishing free women from slave women, so when it is known that a woman is free, she will not be accosted in the way a slave woman is accosted. The meaning is not that the woman should be recognized so that it is known who she is; rather, what is intended is that she be distinguished from a slave woman, because in Medina there were slave women known for wrongdoing, and foolish men would sometimes approach them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 60:

﴿If the hypocrites do not desist﴾ etc.: This includes a warning against these categories if they do not desist. It is said: they did not desist, and the warning was not carried out against them. In this there is evidence for the invalidity of the view that it is obligatory to carry out threats in the Hereafter. It is also said: they did desist and concealed their affair, so the carrying out of the warning was withheld from them. The hypocrites (al-munafiqun) are those who show faith and conceal disbelief. Those in whose hearts is a disease are a people in whom there was weakness of faith and little steadfastness upon it. It is said: they are the fornicators, as in His saying: ﴿so that he in whose heart is a disease might be moved to desire﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32]. ﴿And the agitators in al-Madinah﴾: a people who used to spread news of evil and frighten the Muslims. It is possible that these categories are distinct, or that they are included within the general body of the hypocrites, and then they are singled out for mention. ﴿Then We would surely incite you against them﴾, i.e., We would empower you over them, and this is the warning. ﴿Then they would not remain as your neighbors therein﴾, that is, because He would expel them or kill them. The pronoun in "therein" refers to al-Madinah. ﴿Except for a little﴾: it may be intended to mean except for a little neighboring, or a little time, or a small number of them. The grammatical analysis (i'rab) varies according to these possibilities: "qaliylan" (little) on the first possibility is a verbal noun (masdar); on the second it is an adverb of time (zarf); and on the third it is in the accusative as an exception (istithna').

"Cursed" (mal'unina) is in the accusative of censure, or it is a substitute for "a little" in the third possibility; or it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun of the agent in "yujāwirūnaka" (they dwell near you), its implied sense being: "they will be expelled, cursed." ﴿Wherever they are found, they shall be seized﴾, i.e., wherever they are overtaken and captured, they shall be taken, and "seizing" (al-akhdh) means capture.

Translation:

﴿The way of Allah﴾ means His custom, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿Concerning those who passed away before﴾ means His custom regarding the hypocrites of the earlier nations. It has also been said that it refers to the disbelievers at Badr, because they were taken captive and killed.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verse 63:

﴿It may be that it is soon﴾ He said "qarīban" (soon) in the masculine form, although "al-sā'āt" (the Hours) is feminine, on the assumption of "shay'an qarīban" (a near thing), or "zamānan qarīban" (a near time), or because its feminine gender is not real (ḥaqīqī).

﴿On the Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾. The governing element (al-'amil) of "the Day" is either their saying ﴿they will say﴾ or ﴿they will not find﴾, or it is an omitted verb. The turning over of their faces means directing them toward the direction of the Fire, just as a piece of meat [a morsel] turns about in the cooking pot when it boils, moving from one side to the other, or it means changing them from their former states.

﴿Do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾. They were a people from the Children of Israel (Banu Isra'il). As for their harm to him, what appears in the hadith (a prophetic report) is that the Children of Israel used to bathe naked, and Moses would conceal himself from them when he bathed. So they said: "He has an aadar" [i.e., he has a defect in his testicle]. Moses bathed one day alone and placed his garments on a rock, and the rock fled with his garments. Moses followed it saying: "My garment, rock! My garment, rock!" He passed by an assembly (mala') of the Children of Israel, who saw him free of what they had said. This is His saying: ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said﴾. It was also said that their harm to him was that they accused him of killing his brother Aaron (Harun). So Allah sent angels who carried him until the Children of Israel saw him with no trace of it, and Allah cleared Moses. It is also narrated that Allah revived Aaron, and he informed them of Moses' innocence. The first view is the sound one, because it is reported in the authentic hadith. ﴿A true, upright word﴾. It was said: this means "There is no god but Allah." But the wording is more general than that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 33, verses 72–73:

﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains﴾. The trust (al-amanah) is the legal obligations (al-takalif al-shar'iyyah), namely the commitment to acts of obedience and the abandonment of acts of disobedience. It has also been said that it is the trust concerning wealth: the ritual washing from major impurity (ghusl al-janabah). The sound view is that it is general, covering all obligations. As for offering it to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, this may bear two meanings. The first: God created for them a capacity of perception, and He actually offered them the trust, so they feared it and refused to bear it. The second: the intended meaning is to magnify the importance of the trust, and that it is so heavy that if it were offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, they would have refused to bear it and would have feared it. This is a kind of metaphor (majaz), like your saying: "I offered a great load to the animal, and it refused to carry it," meaning that it is unable to carry it. ﴿But man bore it﴾, that is, man undertook the duty of carrying out the obligations despite their great severity and difficulty for the bodies that are greater than him. For this reason God described him as "wrongdoing and ignorant." Here "man" (al-insan) is a generic noun (jins). It has been said that it refers to Adam, and it has been said that it refers to the one who killed his brother. ﴿So that He may punish﴾: the lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-sayrurah), since bearing the trust became the cause of the punishment of the hypocrites and the polytheists, and a mercy to the believers.
